subject: ventures/dj-gig-profit-calculator
professional: a bookkeeper or CPA for self-employed wedding and mobile DJs (Schedule C filers). What they check first: whether 'take-home' means before or after self-employment and income tax; whether the price floor really reaches the hourly target once overhead is spread over the hours the DJ actually books; whether vehicle cost per mile is near the IRS standard mileage rate for the year; whether gear is costed as wear per gig; and whether the guide's suggested price is anywhere near what the market pays (The Knot's average for a wedding DJ is about $1,700 to $1,800).

evidence.correctness: Recomputed by hand, then compared with the engine output from node /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/81df4cd4-800b-55c5-bc31-b22ef2785d5d/scratchpad/dj/check.mjs /home/user/oss-monorepo/ventures/dj-gig-profit-calculator. Package table: for the sample 'Wedding reception (5h)' (1800, 5 h, $120 cost, setup 2 + prep 1, 3% card fee, $1,100/mo overhead, 25 h/wk x 50 wk), overhead/hour = 13,200/1,250 = 10.56, contribution = 1,746 - 120 = 1,626, /8 = 203.25, profit/hour 192.69, floor ((40+10.56)x8+120)/0.97 = 540.70. Engine: 10.5600 / 192.6900 / 540.7010. Weekly mix (monthly revenue 14,700 x 12/50 = 3,528): own 2,910.96, lead 2,381.76, agency 1,534.80; +10% raise break-even loss 342.216/3,517.176 = 9.7299%, weekly change at 90% retention -9.50. All match. Quote builder: costs 40+10+15+28 = 93, profit 1,071, 107.10/h, break-even 93/0.97 = 95.88, target 693/0.97 = 714.43, overtime floor 60/0.97 = 61.86; annual plan need 60,000+1,500+60x68 = 65,580 / (0.97 x 67) = 1,009.08 off, 1,210.89 peak; ladder 775/925/1,100 with profit 643.75/739.25/759. All match the engine and the guide. Arithmetic is right throughout. Two outputs mislead, kept to 3 not 2 because the page states both limits: the 'price for target' does not reach the target at real utilisation (the sample mix priced at every floor earns $37.15 per hour worked against $40, since overhead is spread over 25 bookable hours and only 19.68 are used). And an add-on line with a quoted '$1,200' is silently split into price 1, cost 200, hours 150 (quote.mjs:45). The package parser was fixed for this on 2026-11-11 and the add-on parser was not.

Pure, small, dependency-free; output goes through esc() or textContent; input validated with clear errors. The copy drifted: splitCells' quoted-comma fix (calc.mjs:148) was never applied to parseAddons (quote.mjs:45). A missing gigs-per-month field silently defaults to 1 (calc.mjs:36).
evidence.claims: Backed: disclaimer, no-warranty, no-SLA and 'Not affiliated' lines on both pages (page.test.mjs, quote.test.mjs:123); no network calls (grep plus tests); the formulas in 'How it is calculated' match calc.mjs; every guide number matches the engine (test plus my recomputation); the page and guide assert no market price, so there is no rate claim to falsify. Unbacked or contradicted: (1) 'Take-home' labels (index.html:79,117,120,263; guide :45,:62,:71) name pre-tax Schedule C profit. On the guide's $60,000 goal, SE tax alone is 60,000 x 0.9235 x 0.153 = $8,477.73, so about $69,873 of profit is needed to keep $60,000 after SE tax. The page's 'Not modelled' line and the README mention SE tax, but the guide never does. (2) The page's 'Not modelled: ... deposits and cancellations, overtime clauses, ... seasonality' (index.html:161) and README:21 contradict the same page's quote builder, which models a deposit schedule, overtime and a peak/off-season split. Source llms.txt carries github.io URLs, which the deploy rewrites (source-only, not filed).
evidence.fitness: Walked a wedding DJ's job: price a 5-hour reception and set an annual plan. The tool gives a clear bottom-up break-even and target price and makes unpaid hours visible, which is the core insight. Gaps a bookkeeper hits in the first hour: (a) no tax set-aside, so the annual goal is pre-tax; (b) the guide titled 'How much should a wedding DJ charge' lands its example at a $714 target. That is about 40% of The Knot's reported national average of roughly $1,700 to $1,800 (theknot.com/content/average-cost-wedding-band-dj, via search), and the guide gives no market anchor or warning that its example is far below typical; (c) lead marketplaces are modelled only as a percent of each booked gig, though The Knot and WeddingWire listings are mostly flat subscriptions and Thumbtack charges per lead; (d) quote-builder overhead is only insurance and software (no marketing, website, phone, music-pool split, vehicle insurance).
evidence.domain: Compared with standard cost-plus pricing and Schedule C practice. Right: units-of-production gear wear (6,000/150 = $40 per gig), fees grossed up as /(1-f), break-even loss with fixed overhead, unpaid-hours accounting. Departures: overhead is allocated over capacity, not expected booked hours, so the floor price under-recovers overhead whenever utilisation is below 100% (documented in the FAQ, but the price is still labelled 'price that hits your hourly target'). There is no SE-tax (15.3% on 92.35%) or income-tax set-aside. The default vehicle cost of $0.70/mile equals the 2025 IRS business standard mileage rate; the 2026 rate is 72.5 cents (IR-2025-128, Notice 2026-10), raised to 76 cents from 2026-07-01 (Announcement 2026-11, via secondary sources). The field is labelled 'what the vehicle really costs you', not as the IRS rate, so this is low severity.

'Price for target' allocates overhead over bookable capacity (25 h/wk), not booked hours. When utilisation is below 100%, pricing every package at its floor misses the target: on the sample mix (79% used), $37.15 per hour worked against $40, while every line shows 'meets'. The allocation is documented in the FAQ, but the label promises the target.

'Take-home' labels (per-hour target, annual goal, 'Take-home profit' row, guide's $60,000 example) are pre-tax Schedule C profit. SE tax alone is $8,477.73 on $60,000 (15.3% x 92.35%), so keeping $60,000 after SE tax needs about $69,873. The guide never mentions tax.

The 'Not modelled' list on the page and README says deposits, overtime clauses and seasonality are not modelled, while the quote builder on the same page models a deposit schedule, overtime and a peak/off-season split.

The guide 'How much should a wedding DJ charge' ends its worked example at a $714 target for a 5-hour reception, about 40% of The Knot's reported national average (~$1,700-1,800), with no market anchor or warning that the invented inputs are low. Lead marketplaces are modelled only as a percent of booked gigs, though The Knot/WeddingWire listings are mostly flat subscriptions and Thumbtack is pay-per-lead.
The atRetention tests use zero gig costs, so a mutant applying retention twice to costs survives.

Default vehicle cost $0.70/mile is the 2025 IRS business rate; the 2026 rate is 72.5 cents (76 cents from 2026-07-01). The field is labelled as real vehicle cost, not the IRS rate, but no source or year is given.
num/money/money2 and the line parser are copied between calc.mjs and quote.mjs (the cause of the add-on comma bug). A missing gigs-per-month field silently defaults to 1.

verdict: The arithmetic is right. Every output I recomputed by hand matches the engine to the cent: the sample wedding line (192.69/h, floor 540.70), the three-model weekly comparison, the raise break-even, the quote (1,071, 107.10/h, break-even 96, target 714, overtime 61.86), the annual plan (1,009/1,211) and the 775/925/1,100 ladder. The 39 tests pass and catch 10 of 11 seeded mutations, and the guide's numbers are tied to the engine by a test. It does not meet the bar, because claims scores 2. 'Take-home' everywhere means pre-tax profit (the $60,000 goal loses $8,478 to SE tax alone). The page's 'Not modelled' list contradicts its own quote builder. The 'price for target' misses the target whenever the DJ books less than full capacity ($37.15 against $40 on the sample). An add-on typed as "$1,200" silently becomes a $1 price. A DJ's bookkeeper would also want a tax set-aside, a market anchor in the wedding-pricing guide (its example lands at ~40% of The Knot's ~$1,700-1,800 average) and subscription-style marketplace costs.
